Chapter 4: Privilege, Responsibility, and the Power to Make a Difference.
Privilege. Now, that's a word that can make just about anyone a little uneasy, right? It’s often easier to pretend it doesn’t exist—or to feel awkward when it’s brought up—especially when it comes with expectations or even guilt. But what if, instead of shying away from it, we saw privilege for what it really is—a tool that, if we’re honest about it, can actually help us do good in the world?
Think about this: imagine someone who grew up with a few built-in advantages. Maybe they had a supportive family, access to a great education, or a network of people who truly cared. At first, all those gifts might have felt like a heavy weight—like there was this pressure to succeed, to prove they deserved everything that had been given. It's so tempting to chalk every win up to hard work alone, and to ignore the role luck played along the way.
But, over time, there's a realization: privilege isn’t something to be embarrassed about. It’s not a guarantee of success, just a place to begin. So, the real question isn’t, “Do I have advantages?” but, “What am I doing with them?” Privilege can be used to build walls that shut people out—or it can open doors so others can step through, too.
Most of the time, people don’t even notice the ways their lives are made easier by things beyond their control. It’s all too easy to take for granted the safety nets, the encouragement, the opportunities that some folks never get. But when you actually recognize your privilege, you can start to use it on purpose. Maybe you advocate for people who don’t have the same resources. Maybe you share what you’ve got, or you help lift up voices that usually go unheard.
There’s a point—sometimes it sneaks up on you—when you realize your success isn’t just about your own effort. It’s part of a much bigger story. Family support, wise mentors, even the kindness of strangers—they all play a role. And in that light, gratitude becomes more than just a nice feeling. It turns into a call to action. It means asking yourself, “How can I give back? How can I use where I am to help someone else?”
Privilege also brings a responsibility to speak up. When you see injustice, staying silent is still a choice. It’s much easier to keep your head down, avoid conflict, and just focus on your own goals. But the people who create real change are the ones who use their privilege as a platform. And you know what? That doesn’t always mean making grand gestures. Sometimes, it’s simply about listening, learning, and choosing to stand with those who are struggling.
All around us, there are people using their advantages to make life better for others. Some do it quietly, just by being generous or kind. Others take bigger risks—challenging unfair systems and speaking out when it really matters. What connects them isn’t just what they have, but how they see it. They believe privilege is more than a gift—it’s a trust.
